title: Where do customers come from?
principle: Find one channel that works, and master it first.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a book called Traction, about how new businesses find customers. Two founders, Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, wrote it. They asked more than 40 founders how they found their first customers. Most people starting out guess this part wrong.

screens.prompt: What do you think most of these founders did to find customers?

options.label: Tried roads until one worked, then stuck to it
Used every road at once, a little of each
Spent most of their money on paid ads

screens.why: Many tried several roads until they found one that worked, then put their effort there. The investor Peter Thiel says in the book that one road is very likely best.

screens.title: The Bullseye framework
screens.text: A channel is a road customers take to find you: WhatsApp groups, Instagram, a café counter, flyers. The book lists 19. Its method is the Bullseye framework, like aiming at the centre of a target: list many, test the best few cheaply, then master the one that works.

screens.prompt: Here are the four steps of the Bullseye framework, mixed up. Put them in order, first one at the top.
steps: List every channel you could use
Pick the three that look most likely
Test each one cheaply for a month
Put most of your effort into the winner
screens.why: Well done. Think wide first, then test a few cheaply, then go deep on the one that works. The test tells you, not your guess.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A tech company and a home bakery both need a road to their customers. It's early May. You bake cakes at home: each ₹850 cake leaves you ₹450. You want 10 new families a month, so last month you tested six roads.

screens.prompt: Here are your six test results. For each one, tell me: keep it in the test, or drop it?

items.text: Posts in colony WhatsApp groups: free, 6 orders
A card on the café counter: free, 3 orders
A hoarding near the station: ₹5,000, 1 order

screens.why: Good. WhatsApp, Instagram and the café card brought orders for little or no money. The others cost ₹2,000 to ₹5,000 for one order or none.

screens.prompt: WhatsApp groups brought 6 orders for free, Instagram 4 for ₹1,000, the café card 3. What do you do next month?

options.label: Spread your time evenly over all three
Put most of your time into WhatsApp groups
Try three new roads to reach new people

screens.why: Right. WhatsApp groups gave the most orders for the least money. Go deeper there: more colonies, better photos, faster replies. Keep the other two small.

wrong.a: That feels fair, but it splits your time three ways. WhatsApp groups gave the most orders for free, so put most of your time there.
wrong.c: You just found a road that works. New roads can wait. WhatsApp groups gave the most orders for free, so go deeper there first.

screens.prompt: Your posts work best in your own colony's group. Why win that group fully before moving to the next colony?

options.label: Happy neighbours there tell the next colony
Twenty groups would cost too much money
Other colonies don't like home bakers

screens.why: Yes. You learned this in Unit 2: win one group first. When a whole colony knows and loves your cakes, they carry your name into the next one.

wrong.b: Joining WhatsApp groups is free. The reason is Unit 2's idea: win one group first, and happy buyers carry your name into the next.
wrong.c: Nothing says they don't. The reason is Unit 2's idea: win one group first, and happy buyers carry your name into the next.

screens.setup: It's mid-May. WhatsApp groups now bring 8 new families a month. A sales agent offers a newspaper insert to 50,000 homes for ₹15,000. Each cake leaves you ₹450.
screens.question: What do you do with your time and money this month?

options.label: Take the insert. It reaches far more homes
options.outcome: The insert brings 3 orders: ₹1,350 for ₹15,000. Busy with the insert, you post less in your WhatsApp groups, and they bring only 5 families this month.
options.why: 50,000 homes sounded big, but your own test showed newspaper inserts bring almost nothing for you.
options.better: Go deeper on WhatsApp: join the groups of the colonies next to yours.

options.label: Split it: a small insert, plus your WhatsApp groups
options.outcome: A ₹5,000 insert brings 1 order. WhatsApp brings 8 families, as before. The insert cost ₹5,000 and earned ₹450 back.
options.why: You kept your best road, but spent money on one your test had already dropped.
options.better: Go deeper on WhatsApp: join the groups of the colonies next to yours.

options.label: Join the groups of the two colonies next to yours
options.outcome: Your neighbours already talk about your cakes in those colonies. With real photos and fast replies, you get 13 new families this month, not 8. That's ₹2,250 more profit, and you spent no money.
options.why: You mastered the road that already works, one colony at a time, before trying new roads.

screens.text: Test a few ___ cheaply, then put most of your effort into the ___ that works.
screens.why: Exactly. That's the Bullseye framework. Your test found WhatsApp groups, and going one colony further brought 13 families instead of 8.

summary: A channel is a road customers take to find you. One channel is often far better than the rest.
The Bullseye framework: list many channels, test the best few cheaply, then master the one that works.
Let test results choose your channel, not how big it sounds.

cards.front: Flyers: ₹2,000 for 1 order. WhatsApp: free, 6 orders. Where do you put your effort?
cards.back: Master the channel that works before adding more.

cards.front: What are the steps of the Bullseye framework?
options: List many, test a few, master one
cards.back: Think wide, test cheaply, then go deep on the winner.

cards.front: An agent offers an ad to 50,000 homes. Your last test of that kind brought nothing. What do you do?
options: Say no and go deeper on what works
cards.back: Your test results choose the channel, not the size of the offer.

sources.label: Gabriel Weinberg and Justin Mares, Traction (Portfolio/Penguin, 2015): publisher's page
